citation: docs/architecture.md, ownership of truth (the core owns composition; cursors are written, not read) and durability (Muster's own durable state is composition, and only composition)
why: Composition is the only thing Muster owns rather than mirrors, which makes it the only thing it can get wrong on its own. Every other picture in the app converges on a daemon's answer eventually; this one has no authority above it to be corrected by. Two properties carry the file. The first is that view-local focus is written and never read back: which pane this window's keyboard feeds is Muster's decision, so another client moving daemon focus must not yank it, and the case that pins that is the one where a reconcile leaves a working focus alone. The second is that composition names daemon things - a tab, a pane - which disappear without asking, and every way they can disappear ends in a window that ignores the keyboard and cannot say why. The cases are written as steps rather than as one call because that is where the bugs are: what a reconcile does to a focus somebody set three steps earlier.

cases.name: a fresh composition is attached to nothing
cases.why: The starting state has to be distinguishable from a window that is set up and showing nothing. No focus at all is the honest answer before a daemon is attached, and the input path reads it as 'this keystroke has nowhere to go' rather than sending it to a pane it invented.

cases.name: a region needs a daemon that is attached
cases.why: A region naming a daemon nobody is connected to renders nothing, forever, and does it silently - there is no pane stream to fail and no error to log. The refusal is returned so the caller says why instead of the window looking broken.

cases.name: the first region takes the keyboard
cases.why: A window with a region in it and no focus ignores the keyboard and cannot say why. The first region opened is the only one it could mean, so it takes focus rather than waiting to be told.

cases.name: a region opened onto a tab picks up its first pane
cases.why: Opening a region says which tab to show; which pane the keyboard feeds is a separate question, and until the daemon has said what is in that tab there is no answer to it. The first reconcile that can see the tab supplies one, so a region opened before the mirror bootstrapped ends up typeable rather than inert.

cases.name: first means first in the tree, not first by id
cases.why: 'The first pane' has to mean the one a user would point at, which is the one the tree puts first. Pane ids are issued in creation order, so a tab whose panes were split in an order other than left-to-right disagrees with them - and id order would put the keyboard in a pane on the far side of the window.

cases.name: a tab whose tree has not arrived still gets a pane
cases.why: herdr publishes a tab's tree on its own event, which may follow the panes it names, so a tab with panes and no tree is an ordinary moment rather than a broken one. A region that waited for the tree would be untypeable for as long as it lasted, and on a quiet tab that is until something else happens.

cases.name: a tree naming a pane the mirror has not got skips it
cases.why: The tree and the pane list arrive on separate events, so a tree can name a pane the mirror has not been told about yet. Pointing the keyboard at one would give the window a focused pane that nothing can render and nothing can type into, which looks exactly like a hung terminal.

cases.name: reconcile leaves a working focus alone
cases.why: Every pane event brings a fresh tree, so reconcile runs constantly. One that re-picked a pane each time would drag the keyboard back to the first pane every time anything in the session moved, which is the same bug as reading daemon focus and just as invisible in a screenshot.

cases.name: a pane whose program exited hands the keyboard back
cases.why: A keyboard pointed at a pane that is gone types into nothing, and says nothing about it - the input path has a pane id and no way to know it is stale. This is the state view-local focus exists to survive, so it resolves here rather than being guarded at every reader.

cases.name: a tab closed from elsewhere closes its region
cases.why: Another client can close the tab this window is showing, and herdr takes its panes with it without announcing them one by one. The region has nothing left to show and no way back, and a window that kept rendering it would be showing a session that does not exist.

cases.name: reconcile answers for one daemon only
cases.why: Streams from different daemons have no mutual order, so what the local daemon just said is no evidence about the devenv's tabs (architecture.md, cross-daemon order is core order). A pass over every region would close a remote region on the strength of a local snapshot - and a dropped VPN would empty the window.

cases.name: detaching a daemon takes its regions and leaves the rest
cases.why: A detached daemon's panes live in a process this window can no longer reach, so its regions have nothing to show. The other daemon's regions are untouched, which is the whole promise of local and remote in one window: losing the tunnel costs the remote half and not the session.

cases.name: closing the focused region moves the keyboard to a survivor
cases.why: Closing a region is a thing the user did, and leaving them with a window that no longer responds to typing is the worst possible answer to it. The first survivor is arbitrary but predictable, and predictable is what a person recovers from.

cases.name: focusing a region that is gone changes nothing
cases.why: A focus intent racing a region that just closed is ordinary - the click was in flight while the daemon said the tab was over - and there is nothing a caller could do about it. Silently keeping the focus that is valid beats clearing it and beats a failure nobody can act on.

cases.name: a region id names one region, ever
cases.why: Ids are what an intent in flight carries. Reusing the number of a closed region would let a keystroke or a divider drag aimed at one region land in whatever took its place, and the two regions may be showing different daemons.

cases.name: attaching a daemon again restates how to reach it
cases.why: Attaching is what happens on every reconnect, and a daemon that came back on a different socket is the same daemon to everyone looking at the window. Adding a second entry would leave two subscriptions to one session and two copies of every pane.

cases.name: a tree that has not caught up does not move the keyboard
cases.why: The pane list and the tree are published separately, so a tab that is mid-split briefly has a tree naming fewer panes than it holds. Reading the tree as evidence that a pane is gone hands the keyboard to another pane and keeps it there, because the tree that arrives a moment later makes the wrong answer valid. It cost an afternoon as a test that passed alone and failed in the suite; the real symptom is a keyboard that jumps to the first pane when you split, sometimes.

cases.name: a zoomed tab shows the one pane, not the tree
cases.why: herdr spells zoom as a flag and keeps publishing every pane at its ordinary unzoomed rect, so a renderer handed the tree paints all of them while the daemon is showing one. Resolving it here rather than flagging it for the shell is what keeps the shell renderable-as-told; the flag survives only so the chrome can say so, because a zoomed tab and a one-pane tab look identical.

cases.name: a view spans daemons, in the order the regions sit
cases.why: One window showing a laptop and a devenv side by side is the desideratum this whole layer exists for, and the view is where it becomes one answer rather than two. Order matters because it is the only part of the arrangement Muster owns - a view that sorted its regions would silently rearrange somebody's window.
